$comment: The broker's local control protocol, as a fixture both languages read. Node: src/control-server.js and bin/handoff-admin.mjs, held against this file by test/control-protocol.test.js. Python (Hermes side, later slices): the drop control client. Nothing here is secret and nothing here is a credential.

transport.exchange: one request line out, one response line back, then the server closes
transport.max_response_bytes_note: The response line every conforming client must be able to buffer. Only `claim` can approach it — base64 of the broker's maxPlaintextBytes (65536 by default) is 87,384 bytes — so it is stated once here rather than derived twice. A client whose reader is smaller does not get to be silent about it: it advertises its real ceiling on `claim` and is refused before anything is consumed.
transport.min_response_bytes_note: The floor under an advertised max_response_bytes; anything smaller is refused with invalid_request. It bounds the `claim` op only, because that is the only op the ceiling applies to: every answer `claim` can give other than a payload — `unavailable` (35 bytes), `invalid_request` (39) and `response_too_large` (114 at its widest, with both counts spelled out in full) — fits inside it, so a conforming client can always read the answer it gets, refusals included. It says nothing about the other ops: a `create` response carrying a rendered notice is ~570 bytes and could grow, which is why transport.max_response_bytes, not this, is the line every client must be able to buffer. A ceiling below this floor could only produce a line the caller cannot read, which would surface as a transport fault for what is really a configuration mistake.
transport.size_convention: Every byte count here is of the whole line as written to the socket, including the terminating newline. That is the unit a reader has to budget for: asyncio's StreamReader, for one, applies its limit to the line plus its separator.

payload_kinds_note: The payload kinds this broker can mint, echoed on every `create` response as `payload_kinds`. Additive and deliberately *not* a protocol version bump: a client that never sends `payload_kind` gets exactly the text drop it always got, and a client that needs file drops reads this list and refuses before posting a link rather than discovering a text-only broker at submit time. Absence of the field means text only. A `text` drop carries one UTF-8 secret under max_plaintext_bytes in envelope v1; a `files` drop carries one HDROP2 container under the file limits in envelope v2, and its bytes are NOT retrievable through `claim` — that is the framed transfer of slice 3 (docs/FILE_TRANSFER_MVP.md).

version_notes.lossless_claim: Version 2 added `max_response_bytes` on `claim`, the `response_too_large` error and `protocol_version` on the `create` response. Only a version 2 broker refuses an oversized claim *before* consuming it; a version 1 broker accepts the field, ignores it, and destroys the payload as it answers. A client therefore reads `protocol_version` rather than assuming the capability from its own age — the field is absent on version 1, and absence means 1.
version_notes.compatibility: Additive. A version 1 client sends no new field and reads no new field, and behaves against a version 2 broker exactly as it did against a version 1 one.

error_notes.invalid_request: A caller mistake: unknown op, missing or ill-typed field, oversized line, unsupported notice_platform, unusable max_response_bytes. Never a statement about a handoff.
error_notes.unavailable: One body for missing, malformed, expired, consumed and lapsed. A content invariant, not a timing one: `await` blocks only for a live pending handoff and therefore leaks liveness to its local caller by construction.
error_notes.response_too_large: `claim` only, and only when the caller advertised a max_response_bytes the answer would not fit in. Nothing is consumed: the payload is untouched, still one-shot, and still claimable by a reader that can hold it until the TTL lapses. Carries required_bytes and max_response_bytes so an operator can act on the mismatch. It is deliberately distinguishable from `unavailable` — it is a statement about the caller's own reader, not about the handoff — and it does tell that caller a payload of that size is waiting. Acceptable for the same reason `await`'s timing leak is: `claim` is reachable only through the 0600 socket, by a caller already trusted with the plaintext.

create.summary: Mint one handoff and return its one-time URL.

ttl_seconds.note: Defaults to the broker's ttlSeconds (1800); must be > 0 and <= maxTtlSeconds (3600).

notice_platform.note: Opt-in. When present, the response also carries notice, notice_received and notice_expired. An unlisted value is refused with invalid_request and mints nothing.

payload_kind.note: Defaults to `text`, which is the drop this protocol has always minted. An unlisted value is refused with invalid_request and mints nothing. A `files` drop additionally reserves its advertised maximum total against the broker's process-wide live-file budget at create time; when that budget is full the creation is refused with the uniform `unavailable` and nothing is minted.

max_files.note: Only meaningful with payload_kind `files`, and refused with invalid_request on a text drop rather than ignored. A positive integer that may only *narrow* the operator's HANDOFF_MAX_FILES; a larger value is clamped down to it. Narrowing the count does not reduce the reservation, because one file may still be the whole per-drop byte total.

response.protocol_version: number: the protocol this broker speaks; absent means 1
response.payload_kinds: array of the payload kinds this broker can mint; absent means ["text"]
response.payload_kind: string: the kind this handoff was minted as, `text` or `files`
response.handoff_id: 22 base64url characters; non-secret and safe to log
response.url: <base>/#<capability> — the capability rides in the fragment and appears nowhere else
response.max_plaintext_bytes: number; text drops only — the secret cap says nothing about a file drop and is not quoted at one
response.max_files: number; files drops only — the count this drop will accept, after any narrowing
response.max_file_bytes: number; files drops only — the per-file cap, with max_total_bytes remaining authoritative
response.max_total_bytes: number; files drops only — the cap this drop reserved against the live-file budget
response.notice: only when notice_platform was given: the waiting message, rendered for that platform
response.notice_received: only when notice_platform was given: the content the waiting message is edited into on submit; identical on every platform
response.notice_expired: only when notice_platform was given: the content it is edited into on lapse; identical on every platform

await.summary: Block on the submission event. Answers with a status and an id, never with the payload.

wait_ms.note: Defaults to 0. The broker never waits past the handoff's own expiry.

claim.summary: Consume the payload exactly once. The only op that returns plaintext. Text drops only: a `files` drop answers `unavailable` here, untouched and still one-shot, because a container is not something to base64 into one newline-delimited line. Its bytes come out over the framed transfer of slice 3.

wait_ms.note: Defaults to 0. When > 0, blocks on the submission event first, so nothing polls.

max_response_bytes.note: The caller's own reader ceiling for one response line in bytes, newline included (see transport.size_convention); must be an integer between transport.min_response_bytes and whatever the caller can really hold. When present the broker sizes the whole response *before* consuming anything and answers response_too_large rather than retire a payload the caller could not have received. Absent means the caller reads an unbounded line and wants no such check — which is what bin/handoff-admin.mjs does, and is why it stays the recovery path for a payload some other reader is too small for. Only honoured by protocol_version 2 and above: a version 1 broker ignores it silently, which is what the version field on `create` is for.

response.plaintext_b64: base64 of the payload bytes — transport encoding for the JSON line, not a protection measure

cli.rule: exit 0 means the payload is waiting: claim it. Any non-zero means do NOT claim.

exit_codes.1: transport failure — socket unreachable, request timed out, or the answer was malformed; the payload's fate is genuinely unknown
exit_codes.2: usage — a caller mistake, never a statement about the handoff
exit_codes.3: the broker answered unavailable: expired, consumed, or the wait lapsed
